meta.generationSource: Wang, Al-Saffar, Rogers & Hahn (2023), Human generation times across the past 250,000 years, Science Advances 9:eabm7047. Sex-averaged generation time 26.9 years (fathers 30.7, mothers 23.2), averaged over the past 250,000 years. https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.abm7047
meta.note: yearsAgo counts back from now; 0 = now, taken as the year 2026. Position along the arms is x = 1 - yearsAgo / spanYears. generationsAgo = yearsAgo / generationYears, rounded. Generations are only literally meaningful inside the humans zone; on the universe and earth zones they answer 'how many human generations would fit'. See research.md for the scale maths, the band tables and the full source list.

zones.label: Earth
zones.note: 4.54 +/- 0.05 Gyr, about 1 per cent. Band boundaries follow the ICS chart.

zones.label: Humans
zones.note: Start set at the hominin/chimpanzee split, about 7 Ma, marked by Sahelanthropus tchadensis (7 to 6 Ma).

bands.label: Recorded history
bands.sourceTitle: The Met: The Origins of Writing

events.label: Big Bang
events.description: Space, time, matter and energy all start here. This is the left fingertip.

events.label: Inflation
events.description: In the first sliver of a second the universe grows enormously. Still theory, but it fits the data.

events.label: First atomic nuclei
events.description: Within minutes protons and neutrons stick together. Nearly all the hydrogen and helium there will ever be is made now.

events.label: The fog clears
events.description: After 380,000 years the gas cools enough for atoms to form and light to travel. We still pick up that light.

events.label: Dark ages
events.description: No stars yet. Just dark, cooling gas pulling itself together.

events.label: First stars
events.description: The first stars switch on. They are the first things to make elements heavier than helium.

events.label: Oldest galaxy we can see
events.description: JADES-GS-z14-0 is the most distant galaxy measured so far. It was already bright 290 million years in.

events.label: The Milky Way starts
events.description: Our own galaxy begins building its thick disc, about 800 million years after the Big Bang.

events.label: Universe turns clear
events.description: Starlight strips the electrons off the hydrogen between galaxies, and the last of the fog lifts.

events.label: A galaxy crashes into ours
events.description: A smaller galaxy falls into the young Milky Way. Its stars are still moving through our sky.

events.label: Peak of star birth
events.description: Stars are being born faster than at any time before or since. The universe is at its brightest.

events.label: Expansion speeds up
events.description: Gravity loses to dark energy, and the universe starts expanding faster instead of slower.

events.label: Solar System forms
events.description: A cloud of gas and dust collapses. The oldest solid grains in any meteorite date from this moment.

events.label: Earth forms
events.description: Our planet clumps together out of the disc around the young Sun.

events.label: The Moon
events.description: Something about the size of Mars hits Earth. The debris becomes the Moon.

events.label: Life
events.description: The oldest structures anyone reads as built by living things. Life shows up early and never stops.

events.label: Oxygen in the air
events.description: Microbes fill the atmosphere with oxygen. For most life at the time it was poison.

events.label: Sex
events.description: Bangiomorpha, a red alga, is the oldest fossil we can date that clearly reproduced sexually.

events.label: Animals everywhere
events.description: In a few tens of millions of years most major animal body plans appear.

events.label: Plants on land
events.description: The first spores from land plants. Green creeps out of the water.

events.label: Legs
events.description: Tiktaalik: a fish with a neck, ribs and the beginnings of arms.
events.sourceTitle: Nature News 2006, on Daeschler et al.

events.label: Dinosaurs die out
events.description: An asteroid hits Mexico. Three quarters of species disappear, and mammals get their chance.

events.label: First primates
events.description: Purgatorius, a mouse-sized climber, appears within a few hundred thousand years of the asteroid.
events.sourceTitle: UC Berkeley Research, on Wilson Mantilla et al. 2021

events.label: Our line splits off
events.description: The whole human story starts here, and it is under a millimetre long on this arm.

events.label: Homo sapiens
events.description: Us. On a 1.90 m span that is four hundredths of a millimetre, thinner than a hair.

events.label: People spread out of Africa
events.description: The move that puts humans on every continent. Invisible at this scale.

events.label: Height of the last ice age
events.description: Ice sheets at their largest, and sea level about 125 m lower than now.

events.label: Farming
events.description: People start growing their food. Everything we call civilisation follows.

events.label: Writing
events.description: Clay tablets in Uruk. All of recorded history is a hundredth of a hair's width on this arm.
events.sourceTitle: The Met: The Origins of Writing

events.label: Great Pyramid
events.description: The oldest building most people can name.

events.label: Roman Empire
events.description: Two thousand years ago sits about a quarter of a micrometre from the fingertip.

events.label: First telescope views
events.description: Galileo publishes what he saw: moons around Jupiter, mountains on the Moon.

events.label: We learn the universe expands
events.description: Hubble shows distant galaxies are moving away. The universe gets a beginning, and an age.

events.label: The Big Bang's echo is found
events.description: Penzias and Wilson pick up the microwave glow left over from the fog clearing.

events.label: People on the Moon
events.description: The furthest anyone has been from the fingertip they are standing on.

events.label: The length of this arm is measured
events.description: The Planck satellite's final results fix the age of the universe at 13.787 billion years.

events.label: Webb telescope opens its eye
events.description: The telescope that found the most distant galaxy on this arm starts work.

events.label: Earth forms
events.description: Dust and rock around the young Sun clump into a planet. This is the left fingertip.

events.label: The Moon is made
events.description: A Mars-sized body hits Earth. The splash cools into the Moon.

events.label: Oldest piece of Earth
events.description: A zircon crystal from the Jack Hills, Australia. Its chemistry says there was already liquid water.

events.label: Oceans
events.description: Surface water, far earlier than anyone expected for a planet this young.

events.label: Oldest whole rock
events.description: The Acasta Gneiss in Canada. The Archean eon is defined to begin with it.

events.label: First life
events.description: Layered mounds in Greenland rock, read as built by microbes. Contested, but nothing older is on offer.

events.label: First fossils most people accept
events.description: Microbial mats in the Dresser Formation, Western Australia.

events.label: Life learns to use sunlight
events.description: Photosynthesis without oxygen comes first, and runs the biosphere for a billion years.

events.label: Oxygen-making microbes
events.description: Cyanobacteria start splitting water and letting the oxygen go. The waste product remakes the planet.

events.label: Great Oxidation Event
events.description: Oxygen rises in the air. It only becomes permanent about 2.22 billion years ago.

events.label: Earth freezes over
events.description: The Huronian glaciations. Oxygen eats the methane that kept the planet warm.

events.label: First big supercontinent
events.description: Columbia, also called Nuna. Continents have been gathering and splitting ever since.

events.label: Sex, and complex cells
events.description: Bangiomorpha, a red alga: the oldest datable fossil of a complex cell that reproduced sexually.

events.label: Rodinia
events.description: A supercontinent that sat across the equator, then broke apart.

events.label: Snowball Earth
events.description: Ice reaches the tropics, twice. The Cryogenian period is named for it.

events.label: Ediacaran begins
events.description: The ice retreats, and the first large organisms follow.

events.label: First large animals
events.description: Fronds and discs on the sea floor. Nothing much like them survives today.

events.label: Cambrian explosion
events.description: Shells, eyes, guts, legs. Most animal body plans appear in a geological blink.

events.label: First fish
events.description: Myllokunmingia from Chengjiang, China: a jawless fish, and the oldest thing with a backbone.

events.label: Plants move onto land
events.description: The first land-plant spores. Nothing bigger than a moss for a long time yet.

events.label: Ordovician extinction
events.description: The first of the big five. Ice caps grow, sea level drops, most marine species die.

events.label: First animals on land
events.description: Pneumodesmus, a millipede from Scotland, with holes in its shell for breathing air.

events.label: First forests
events.description: Archaeopteris, a tree with real roots and a trunk. Roots start making real soil.

events.label: Fish with arms
events.description: Tiktaalik has a neck, ribs and shoulders. The arm this whole site is drawn on starts here.
events.sourceTitle: Nature News 2006, on Daeschler et al.

events.label: Late Devonian extinction
events.description: A long series of die-offs in the sea, ending the Devonian.

events.label: Pangaea
events.description: Nearly all the land in one piece, from pole to pole.

events.label: Eggs that need no pond
events.description: Amniote eggs carry their own water, so animals can finally live away from water.

events.label: Coal forests collapse
events.description: The great swamps dry out. Their buried wood is the coal we later burned.

events.label: The Great Dying
events.description: The worst extinction there has ever been. Around 80 per cent of marine species gone.

events.label: First dinosaurs
events.description: Nyasasaurus from Tanzania is either the oldest dinosaur or its closest relative.
events.sourceTitle: UCMP Berkeley, on Nesbitt et al. 2013

events.label: First mammals
events.description: Brasilodon, a shrew-sized animal in Brazil with mammal teeth. It lived beside the first dinosaurs.

events.label: Triassic extinction
events.description: Volcanism as Pangaea starts to split. It clears the way for dinosaurs to take over.

events.label: The Atlantic opens
events.description: Pangaea splits and a new ocean starts widening. It is still widening today.

events.label: First birds
events.description: Archaeopteryx in the Solnhofen limestone: feathers, wings, and a mouth full of teeth.

events.label: Flowers
events.description: Flowering plants appear, then take over the land in about 50 million years.

events.label: Mammals with placentas
events.description: Eomaia, from China, is the oldest fossil on the branch that leads to us.

events.label: Asteroid, end of the dinosaurs
events.description: A 10 km rock hits Yucatan. Three quarters of species go, and the Mesozoic ends.

events.label: First primates
events.description: Purgatorius, a small climber in Montana, only a hundred thousand years or so after the asteroid.
events.sourceTitle: UC Berkeley Research, on Wilson Mantilla et al. 2021

events.label: A sudden hot spell
events.description: Carbon floods the air and the world warms 5 to 8 degrees. The closest thing to what we are doing now.

events.label: Primates spread worldwide
events.description: Teilhardina turns up in Asia, Europe and North America within a few thousand years.

events.label: Mammals go back to sea
events.description: Pakicetus and its relatives walk into the water and become whales.

events.label: India hits Asia
events.description: The collision that is still pushing the Himalaya up a few millimetres a year.

events.label: Antarctica freezes
events.description: A permanent ice sheet forms in the south. The long cooling towards our ice ages begins.

events.label: First apes
events.description: Tailless, big-brained primates in Africa. Our own branch of the family.

events.label: Grasslands spread
events.description: Grasses take over dry country. Grazing animals follow, and later so do our ancestors.

events.label: Our line splits from chimpanzees
events.description: Where the humans timeline starts, and 2.9 mm from the right fingertip on this one.

events.label: The Mediterranean refills
events.description: The sea had dried down to salt flats. Water pours back in through Gibraltar.

events.label: Panama closes
events.description: North and South America join. Ocean currents change, and animals swap continents.

events.label: Genus Homo
events.description: A jaw from Ledi-Geraru, Ethiopia: the oldest fossil most researchers call Homo.

events.label: The ice ages begin
events.description: The Quaternary. Ice sheets grow and shrink on a cycle, and never quite go away.

events.label: Homo sapiens
events.description: Fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco. Our whole species is 0.13 mm on this arm.

events.label: Height of the last ice age
events.description: Ice over half of Europe and North America, and sea level 125 m lower.

events.label: Holocene begins
events.description: The warm spell we still live in. Everything humans built happened inside it.

events.label: Farming
events.description: One species starts reshaping the surface of the planet on purpose.

events.label: Industrial era
events.description: Coal, then oil. Carbon that took 300 million years to bury goes back into the air.

events.label: We start measuring the air
events.description: Continuous CO2 records begin at Mauna Loa. The line has gone up every year since.

events.label: Split from chimpanzees
events.description: Our line and the chimpanzee line part. Sahelanthropus, from Chad, sits about here.

events.label: Orrorin
events.description: Leg bones from Kenya, suggesting an ape that already walked upright.

events.label: Ardipithecus kadabba
events.description: Teeth and toe bones from Ethiopia. Still very ape-like.

events.label: Ardi
events.description: Ardipithecus ramidus: a nearly complete skeleton. It climbed trees and walked on the ground.

events.label: First Australopithecus
events.description: Australopithecus anamensis. Walking upright is now the normal way to get around.

events.label: Footprints at Laetoli
events.description: Two or three individuals walk across wet ash in Tanzania. The stride is human.

events.label: Kenyanthropus
events.description: A flat-faced skull from Kenya. The family tree is a bush, not a ladder.

events.label: Oldest stone tools
events.description: Sharp flakes struck at Lomekwi, Kenya, 700,000 years before anyone in our own genus existed.

events.label: Australopithecus africanus
events.description: The southern African branch, and the first early human fossil ever found in Africa.

events.label: Lucy
events.description: Australopithecus afarensis. One metre tall, brain the size of a chimpanzee's, fully upright.

events.label: Genus Homo
events.description: A lower jaw from Ledi-Geraru, Ethiopia. Smaller teeth, and a hint of what is coming.

events.label: Oldowan toolkit
events.description: Hammerstones and sharp flakes for cutting meat off bone. The same design for a million years.

events.label: Paranthropus
events.description: Huge jaws and chewing muscles for tough plants. A cousin, not an ancestor.

events.label: Homo habilis
events.description: A bigger brain and a smaller face. Found with stone tools, which is how it got its name.

events.label: Homo erectus
events.description: Long legs, our body shape, and the first of us to leave Africa. It lasted almost two million years.

events.label: Out of Africa, first time
events.description: Skulls at Dmanisi in Georgia. Humans are in Europe long before Homo sapiens exists.

events.label: Hand axes
events.description: A tool shaped to a plan, and the same plan everywhere for over a million years.

events.label: Homo antecessor
events.description: Fossils from Atapuerca in Spain, near the base of the European branch.

events.label: Cooking on fire
events.description: Hearths with burnt seeds and fish. Cooked food is easier to digest and feeds a bigger brain.

events.label: Homo heidelbergensis
events.description: Big-brained and big-bodied, and the likely common ancestor of us and the Neanderthals.

events.label: Neanderthals split off
events.description: Their line and ours part. They go north into Europe and Asia, we stay in Africa.

events.label: Homo naledi
events.description: A small-brained human deep in a South African cave, far more recent than its skull suggests.

events.label: Homo sapiens
events.description: Fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco. Our own species, about 11,700 generations back.

events.label: Wooden hunting spears
events.description: Nine spears and a horse kill site at Schoningen, Germany. Redated in 2025 from 300,000 to 200,000 years.

events.label: Oldest jewellery
events.description: Pierced Tritia gibbosula sea-snail shells from Bizmoune Cave, Morocco, worn as beads. Someone wanted to be seen.

events.label: A paint workshop
events.description: Ground ochre mixed and stored in shells at Blombos Cave, South Africa.

events.label: Burying the dead
events.description: Deliberate graves at Qafzeh and Skhul in Israel, some with objects placed in them.

events.label: Denisovans
events.description: A whole human population known mostly from DNA. Their genes are still in people today.

events.label: People reach Australia
events.description: Madjedbebe, northern Australia. Getting there needed boats and open-water crossings.

events.label: The move that peopled the world
events.description: Everyone alive outside Africa descends mostly from this one dispersal. About 2,200 generations ago.

events.label: Oldest picture of a story
events.description: A cave wall in Sulawesi shows human figures and a wild pig, doing something together.

events.label: Modern humans in Europe
events.description: We arrive in a continent Neanderthals have had to themselves for hundreds of thousands of years.

events.label: Neanderthals end
events.description: The last of them, after two to five thousand years of living alongside us.

events.label: Chauvet Cave
events.description: Horses, lions and rhinos drawn in charcoal by people who clearly knew how to draw.

events.label: Oldest fired clay figure
events.description: The Venus of Dolni Vestonice. Fired clay used for art long before anyone made pots.

events.label: People in the Americas
events.description: Footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, from the middle of the ice age. Still argued over.

events.label: Oldest pots
events.description: Fired clay vessels in Xianrendong Cave, China, ten thousand years before farming.

events.label: Height of the last ice age
events.description: Small, scattered groups of people, and ice over much of the north.

events.label: Dogs
events.description: Wolves that stayed near our camps become another species. The first animal we lived with.

events.label: The climate settles
events.description: The ice age ends. A warm, steady climate for the first time in a hundred thousand years.

events.label: Gobekli Tepe
events.description: Carved stone circles in Turkey, built by people who had not started farming yet.
events.sourceTitle: German Archaeological Institute: dating Gobekli Tepe

events.label: Farming
events.description: Wild cereals become crops in southwest Asia. About 430 generations ago.

events.label: Herds
events.description: Goats and sheep first, then cattle and pigs. Food that walks with you.

events.label: The wheel
events.description: A wagon scratched on a clay pot at Bronocice, Poland, is among the oldest evidence.

events.label: Writing
events.description: Clay tablets at Uruk, counting grain and labour. Recorded history is 197 generations long.
events.sourceTitle: The Met: The Origins of Writing

events.label: Great Pyramid
events.description: Built about 171 generations ago, by a state that could feed and organise thousands.

events.label: The alphabet
events.description: Proto-Sinaitic: one sign per sound. Writing becomes something ordinary people can learn.

events.label: Roman Empire
events.description: About 74 generations ago. Closer to us than to the first writing.

events.label: Printing press
events.description: Gutenberg's movable type. Ideas start travelling faster than the people carrying them.

events.label: The Atlantic crossing
events.description: Two halves of the world that had been apart for 15,000 years meet again.

events.label: Industrial Revolution
events.description: Coal and steam, about nine generations ago. It changed the whole planet.

events.label: Vaccination
events.description: Jenner's smallpox vaccine. The first disease we would go on to wipe out.

events.label: On the Origin of Species
events.description: The book that explains everything on the left half of this arm.

events.label: Powered flight
events.description: Twelve seconds at Kitty Hawk. Sixty-six years later, the Moon.

events.label: Antibiotics
events.description: Fleming's mould. Infection stops being a normal way to die.

events.label: The double helix
events.description: We work out how the instructions are written down, and later how to read them.

events.label: People on the Moon
events.description: Roughly two generations ago.

events.label: The World Wide Web
events.description: Written down as a proposal in 1989, just over one generation ago.

events.label: The human genome is read
events.description: Three billion letters, most of them far older than this whole arm.

events.label: Eight billion people
events.description: More humans alive at once than in any generation before.
